rv.q: In essence, Fahmy has a terrific setting and concept for a great play, but not yet that play.

This really does seem like the classic but unfortunate case of what can happen when writers direct their own work: a production that seems in love with the words being spoken and not the dramatic events they exist to create.
Fahmy's A Distinct Society is a candid, provocative look into how this ban tragically affected millions of Muslims, leaving them helpless and afraid.
Fahmy’s words and direction are a beautifully balanced equation of the confusion, anger, and raw emotion of bigotry and nationalism.
A Distinct Society is definitely a recommended evening of theater.
Her performance takes the play to a higher level.
The play fares best when Fahmy keeps the focus there and not on a romantic subplot that is unconvincing and only clutters the narrative.
It needs tightening and focus, but the story Fahmy is trying to tell is important and rich with dramatic potential.
I think it is, in its current form, underbaked, but there are many things I liked a lot.
What we get is a cluttered, disjointed and melodramatic theatrical experience that fails not only to make a clear statement of protest and outrage, but also to hold our attention as an audience.

It is in fact deeply moving and when the final scene begins, you will see how these players have been transformed into different people than they were at the start of the story, only 95 minutes earlier.
The bones of a great story are there with “A Distinct Society.”

cn.t: This timely drama about the Muslim ban and border separation earns praise for its compelling premise and human focus, but critics find the execution uneven, with some calling it sluggish and incomplete despite strong intentions.
